extracted.intended_audience: prospective NSF GRFP applicants (early-stage graduate/PhD students in STEM)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing a competitive NSF Graduate Research Fellowship application, focusing on the two required essays (Personal, Relevant Background and Future Goals; and Graduate Research Plan) and meeting NSF review criteria and formatting requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the NSF GRFP Program Solicitation exactly
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the official NSF GRFP Program Solicitation right away; it contains eligibility, deadlines, how to apply, review criteria, and formatting rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Program Solicitation is a self-contained document with all essential information. Failure to follow formatting guidelines can result in desk rejection. Read it early to avoid mistakes (the author discovered late that her essay formatting was wrong).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary effort on the two required essays
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of your application outcome depends on prior accomplishments, but your main efforts should be directed toward the two required essays: the Personal, Relevant Background and Future Goals Statement (max 3 pages) and the Graduate Research Plan Statement (max 2 pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal statement = 'how I got here and where I'm going' (max 3 pages). Graduate Research Plan = short proposal demonstrating ability to pitch an impactful project, understand literature, and plan/evaluate execution (max 2 pages). You do not necessarily have to carry out the exact plan if awarded, but you must convincingly show feasibility, impact, and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Merit (NSF review criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate the potential to advance knowledge — the scientific impacts of your past, present, and future research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address questions such as: What scientific contributions have you made or will you make? What knowledge gaps does your research fill? How can other researchers build on your work? What tangible outcomes (publications, presentations) or honors have you received? In the Personal Statement discuss Intellectual Merits of previous projects (novel methodologies, promising results, publications, presentations, awards). The Graduate Research Plan should be primarily about Intellectual Merit: emphasize novelty of methods and importance of the problem. Use concrete examples (e.g., thesis that became an accepted conference paper and reviewer comment indicating likely uptake by others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts (NSF review criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the potential of your research and activities to benefit society and contribute to desired societal outcomes; show how research goes beyond academia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider: How can you make your research accessible to a broad audience? How have you or will you communicate your work to the public? Who benefits and how? In the Personal Statement, highlight teaching and outreach (especially activities increasing minority participation in STEM) or evidence your research has been used 'in the wild.' In the Graduate Research Plan, describe societal impacts and public engagement plans; impacts can be indirect and you can discuss plans to communicate results. The author's example: Broader Impacts paragraph included outreach and teaching experience, and the proposal had sentences about both societal impacts and public engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide concrete evidence of past accomplishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Make tangible outcomes visible: publications, presentations, awards, novel methodologies, promising experimental results, and endorsements from other scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing previous work, cite outcomes (accepted papers, talks), mention reviewer or community endorsements when possible, and explicitly state how others can build on your work. Bold or otherwise highlight key results and awards to draw reviewer attention. Reviewers look for demonstrated productivity and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research plan content and structure expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Graduate Research Plan should motivate the problem, present the proposed approach and evaluation plan, and summarize intellectual merit and broader impacts within the page limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested structure (from author's example): motivations and notation (~1/3 page), proposed approach and evaluation plan (~1 page), intellectual merit and technical contributions (~1/3 page), and broader societal/outreach impacts (~1/3 page). Include an evaluation plan so reviewers can judge feasibility and rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly map your materials to NSF review criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly demonstrate how you and your research fulfill the GRFP's two review criteria (Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call out criteria-relevant information within essays (e.g., label subsections or sentences that state Intellectual Merit / Broader Impacts). Being explicit helps busy reviewers quickly find evidence. The author split project descriptions into Intellectual Merits and Broader Impacts subsections in her Personal Statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation, style, and clarity to help busy reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Write in a way that makes important information easy to find: be specific, use figures if helpful, and highlight key results/awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bold important results, awards, and contributions to draw attention. Use figures if they clarify your research. The NSF has a specific 'style'—try to match it. Reviewers read many applications, so concise, well-signposted writing improves chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit appropriate reviewers for feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Get many people to read your essays, prioritizing past fellowship winners and faculty experienced in writing NSF proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most valuable reviewers are past fellowship winners and professors who understand NSF expectations and style. Their feedback helps align your essays with reviewer priorities and avoid implicit mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid underselling yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let imposter syndrome lead you to downplay your scientific value; emphasize your contributions heavily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not the place to show self-doubt. Highlight your achievements and the significance of your work rather than minimizing them.
